name: tomato tart
instructions:
From America's Test Kitchen. A savory tomato tart on a press-in tart shell, built on a three-cheese base (parmesan + ricotta + mozzarella) with shingled tomatoes on top, drizzled with garlic-oil, and finished with basil. Two variations from ATK's original: zucchini tart (sub for tomatoes) and mushroom tart (omit tomatoes and garlic-oil, use sautéed thyme-and-garlic mushrooms instead). Serves 4-6.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 3 plum tomatoes, cored and sliced 1/4 inch thick
- salt and pepper
- 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
- 1 garlic clove, minced
- 1 oz Parmesan cheese, grated (1/2 cup)
- 4 oz (1/2 cup) part-skim ricotta cheese (or whole-milk ricotta — see notes; do NOT use fat-free)
- 1 oz mozzarella cheese, shredded (1/4 cup)
- 1 baked and cooled tart shell (ATK's All-Butter Press-In Tart Dough — see savory-pie-crust for a comparable base)
- 2 tbsp chopped fresh basil (for finish, off heat)

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. SALT AND DRAIN THE TOMATOES: spread the sliced tomatoes out over several layers of paper towels, sprinkle with 1/2 tsp salt, and let drain for 30 minutes. This is the load-bearing moisture-control step — see notes.
2. Meanwhile, in a small bowl combine 2 tbsp of the olive oil with the minced garlic. Set aside.
3. In a separate bowl, combine the Parmesan, ricotta, mozzarella, and the remaining 1 tbsp olive oil. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
4. Adjust oven rack to middle position and heat oven to 425°F.
5. Spread the ricotta cheese mixture evenly over the baked tart shell.
6. Blot the drained tomatoes dry with paper towels. Shingle them attractively on top of the ricotta in concentric circles, starting from the outer edge and working in.
7. Drizzle the garlic-oil mixture over the shingled tomatoes.
8. (Tart can be held at room temperature for up to 2 hours before baking.)
9. BAKE: place the tart on a rimmed baking sheet and bake at 425°F until bubbling and the tomatoes are slightly wilted, 20 to 25 minutes, rotating the sheet halfway through.
10. COOL: let the tart cool on the baking sheet for at least 10 minutes (or up to 2 hours).
11. SERVE: remove the outer metal ring of the tart pan, slide a thin metal spatula between tart and tart pan bottom, and carefully slide the tart onto a serving platter or cutting board. Sprinkle with chopped fresh basil before serving.

=== VARIATIONS (FROM ATK) ===

ZUCCHINI TART: substitute 1 large zucchini, sliced into 1/4-inch-thick rounds, for the tomatoes. Salt zucchini as directed in step 1 (same 30-minute drain).

MUSHROOM TART: omit the tomatoes AND the garlic-oil drizzle. Heat 1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil in a 12-inch nonstick skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add 1 lb white button mushrooms (or cremini), sliced thin, and 1/2 tsp salt; cook until mushrooms are lightly browned, about 15 min. Stir in 2 tsp minced fresh thyme and 1 minced garlic clove; cook until fragrant, about 1 minute longer. Spoon the mushroom mixture over the ricotta mixture and bake the tart as directed.
notes:
From America's Test Kitchen — captured from source.

=== MUST BE A TART, NOT A PIE — FORMAT IS LOAD-BEARING ===

Make this in a TART pan, not a pie pan. Tart pans have a shallow height and a removable ring; pie pans are deeper and steeper. If you use a pie pan the filling ends up too thick — the cheese-base + tomato ratio the recipe is engineered around depends on the shallow tart-pan format spreading the filling thin. In a deeper pie pan you get a wet cheese-heavy filling that doesn't set the same way and doesn't have enough tomato coverage per bite.

The removable-ring tart-pan format also matters for serving (step 11 of the procedure — sliding the tart off the pan bottom onto a platter). A pie pan doesn't let you do this cleanly.

=== CHEESE ROLES — BULK VS STRUCTURE (THE THREE CHEESES DO DIFFERENT JOBS) ===

The cheese mixture has real flexibility, but the roles matter:

- BULK CHEESE (RICOTTA OR COTTAGE CHEESE) IN A FOOD PROCESSOR: this is the volume of the base. Ricotta is ATK's choice; cottage cheese also works. Processing in a food processor smooths out the curds and gives you the creamy spreadable base the recipe wants — chunky ricotta or unblended cottage cheese would leave visible grainy texture.

- STRUCTURE CHEESES (PARMESAN + MOZZARELLA) FOR LESS-RUNNY + SALT: parmesan and mozzarella (or similar structural/salty cheeses) do two jobs on top of the bulk: (1) they add salt and umami that the bulk cheeses alone don't carry, and (2) they add binding/structure that keeps the finished base from reading too runny under the tomatoes.

So the mix isn't just 'three cheeses for depth' — it's bulk + structure + salt, and you can swap within each category (cottage cheese for ricotta on the bulk side; other salty melting cheeses for parmesan/mozzarella on the structure side).

=== ATK'S HEADNOTE (WHY THIS RECIPE WORKS) ===

ATK's framing: tomato tarts sound promising but often yield soggy crusts and fillings with very little flavor. Their approach:
- FOOLPROOF CRUST + CREAMY BASE + FRAGRANT SLICED TOMATOES: goal was a simple recipe that avoids the soggy-crust / bland-filling failure mode.
- SALT-AND-DRAIN THE TOMATOES FIRST: 30 minutes on paper towels with salt to leach moisture out before they ever touch the tart shell. This is the whole soggy-crust prevention.
- TRIO OF CHEESES AS A BASE LAYER: Parmesan + ricotta + mozzarella combined with olive oil into a cheese base under the tomatoes. The cheese layer acts as a moisture buffer between the crust and the tomatoes.
- GARLIC-OIL DRIZZLE OVER THE TOMATOES: keeps the tomatoes from drying out during the bake AND infuses them with garlic flavor.

=== SALT-AND-DRAIN THE TOMATOES — LOAD-BEARING MOISTURE CONTROL ===

The 30-min salt-and-drain step is the whole trick that separates this tart from the standard soggy failure mode. Sliced tomatoes on paper towels + 1/2 tsp salt scattered on top → the salt draws moisture out of the tomato flesh, and the paper towels absorb it. Skip this step and you get a wet crust and a wet cheese base after baking. Don't shortcut it — 30 minutes is the target.

BLOT DRY BEFORE SHINGLING: after the 30-min drain, blot the tomatoes with more paper towels before laying them on the tart. Any remaining surface water will bake into the cheese base and defeat the drain step.

=== THE THREE-CHEESE BASE LAYER — MOISTURE BUFFER + FLAVOR ===

Parmesan + ricotta + mozzarella combined with a tablespoon of olive oil is the cheese base. Each contributes something different:
- PARMESAN: sharp umami depth.
- RICOTTA: soft creamy body — the bulk of the base.
- MOZZARELLA: melty stretchy character.

The base does two jobs at once: (1) provides the primary flavor of the tart alongside the tomato, and (2) acts as a moisture buffer between the crust and the tomatoes, keeping the crust from going soggy.

RICOTTA — PART-SKIM PREFERRED, WHOLE-MILK ACCEPTABLE, NEVER FAT-FREE: ATK specifically calls for part-skim ricotta as the preferred choice (lighter flavor). Whole-milk ricotta can be substituted. FAT-FREE RICOTTA IS EXPLICITLY OUT — ATK says do not use it. Fat-free ricotta doesn't set the same way and reads gluey.

=== SHINGLE TOMATOES CONCENTRICALLY — PRESENTATION MATTERS ===

ATK's method: shingle the tomato slices in overlapping concentric circles starting from the outer edge and working toward the center. This is the presentation move — the tart is visually a shingled pattern, not a random scatter. Worth the 2 extra minutes of arrangement.

=== GARLIC-OIL DRIZZLE OVER THE TOMATOES — DUAL ROLE ===

The 2-tablespoon olive oil + minced garlic drizzle (mixed separately, poured over the shingled tomatoes just before baking) does two things:
- KEEPS THE TOMATOES FROM DRYING OUT during the 20-25 min bake at 425°F.
- INFUSES THEM WITH GARLIC FLAVOR from the oil-soluble compounds.

Don't skip. Don't just brush plain olive oil — the garlic infusion is part of the point.

DON'T PUT THE GARLIC IN THE CHEESE BASE — DRIZZLE-ON-TOP ONLY: confirmed on my own cooks that the drizzle-on-top format is better than trying to put the garlic in the cheese base. Garlic in the body won't cook out all the way during the 20-25 min bake — you end up with under-cooked raw-garlic bite scattered through the base. On top, the garlic-and-oil sits in a shallow layer on the tomatoes where the oven heat can actually cook the garlic through and infuse the tomato surface at the same time. ATK got this right.

=== BAKE UNTIL BUBBLING AND JUST-WILTED — DON'T OVERCOOK ===

20-25 min at 425°F. Signs it's done: cheese base bubbling around the edges, tomatoes slightly wilted (not collapsed). Overcooking dries the tomatoes past the wilted-but-intact stage and pushes the cheese base into over-browned territory. Rotate the sheet halfway for even bake.

=== BASIL OFF HEAT, AT THE FINISH — CRUDE BASIL PESTO OVER PLAIN LEAVES ===

Basil goes on AFTER the tart comes out of the oven — off heat, always. Same rule as anywhere basil shows up in this cookbook (see marcella frittata, italian-tomato-white-beans, master-italian-green-sauce-and-pesto) — basil cooked into a dish reads stale and muddy; basil off heat stays bright and green.

UPGRADE: FINISH WITH A CRUDE BASIL PESTO INSTEAD OF PLAIN LEAVES: chopped-basil-scattered-on-top (ATK's default) is fine but a small amount of crude basil pesto — mortar-pounded basil + olive oil + garlic + parmesan, kept rustic and coarse (see master-italian-green-sauce-and-pesto variant A) — drizzled over the finished tart reads distinctly better. The pesto's fat coats every bite instead of the basil sitting as discrete flecks; the extra garlic and cheese in the pesto add another dimension against the tomato-and-cheese-base body of the tart. Crude/coarse specifically — don't puree smooth. Just enough processing to break the basil down and let the oil coat everything.

=== CAN BE HELD BEFORE BAKING ===

ATK notes the assembled-but-unbaked tart can sit at room temperature for up to 2 hours before baking. Useful for dinner parties — do the drain + assembly ahead, bake right before serving.

=== VARIATIONS ===

ZUCCHINI TART: 1 large zucchini sliced 1/4-inch thick, salt-and-drained same as the tomatoes. Everything else identical. Same soggy-crust logic applies — zucchini is even wetter than tomatoes, so the drain is doubly important.

MUSHROOM TART: skip the tomatoes AND the garlic-oil drizzle entirely. Sauté 1 lb sliced mushrooms with salt in olive oil until browned (~15 min), then stir in thyme + garlic. Spoon the sautéed mushrooms over the cheese base and bake as directed. The dry-sauté handles the moisture problem for mushrooms (which release even more water than tomatoes if left raw).

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- master-tartine: open-face bread + spread + toppings. Different structural format (bread base, no pastry, no shingle-and-bake) but similar 'simple ingredients on a base' logic.
- mushroom-leek-galette: another french-adjacent savory pastry with mushrooms. Different format (rustic folded galette vs press-in tart pan).
- french-quiche: another savory pastry-shell format with a cheese-and-egg base. Different filling logic (custard vs cheese-spread + shingled vegetables).
